study.title: 2 Kings 17 - the fall of Israel and the mixed religion of Samaria
study.overview: This chapter closes the history of the Northern kingdom. First, he narrates the end of Hosea, the fall of Samaria and the exile of Israel to Assyria. Then the narrator explains that destruction was not merely a military result, but God's judgment on persistent infidelity: idolatry, imitation of nations, rejection of the covenant and contempt for the prophets. Finally, he describes the population brought by Assyria to occupy Samaria and shows the formation of a hybrid religion: these nations feared the LORD in a partial way, but they continued to serve their idols themselves.

outline.title: Hosea, the siege of Samaria and the deportation
outline.explanation: The last king of Israel appears as a vassal of Assyria, then suspected of treason and imprisoned. Samaria is surrounded for three years and finally taken; the people are deported to regions of Assyria and fears. The text presents this defeat as the historical outcome of the Northern realm.

outline.title: The Spiritual Causes of Fall
outline.explanation: The narrator enumerates the sins of Israel: fear of other gods, adoption of the customs of nations, altars and images everywhere, idolatrous worship and abominable practices. Even after repeated warnings of the prophets, the people hardened the cerviz. The result is the holy wrath of the LORD, who removes them from his presence.

outline.title: Judah follows the same way and Israel is rejected
outline.explanation: Judah is also included in the warning, because he did not keep the commandments of the LORD, but followed the statutes of Israel. The text connects the national ruin to the ancient sin of Jeroboam, who diverted Israel. The deportation to Assyria fulfills what God had said through the prophets.

outline.title: Samaria repopulated and cult mixed
outline.explanation: Assyria installs other peoples in the cities of Samaria. As these groups are unaware of the way to fear the God of the earth, a priest is sent to instruct them. Still, each nation retains its own gods and its own rituals. The end result is a syncretic religion: they fear the Lord at the same time as they serve idols.

study.context: The chapter describes the collapse of the Northern kingdom, called Israel, and the seizure of Samaria by Assyria. The given notes place Hosea as the last king of that kingdom and show that the population was deported, while other peoples were brought to inhabit the land. The text also preserves the memory of how the new population tried to learn something about the Lord, but without abandoning their own cults.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter is clear: God rules history and judges the infidelity of his people. The fall of Israel is not only attributed to Assyrian force, but mainly to persistent sin against the covenant. The text insists that idolatry is not a secondary detail; it is rebellion against the God who has freed Israel from Egypt. The role of the prophets also appears as witnesses of divine patience: there was warning, called to repentance, and refusal to hear. In the end, the chapter exposes the impossibility of dividing religious loyalty: fearing the Lord and continuing to worship idols is a form of infidelity, not of true worship.

scholarViews.insight: The cult rebuilt in Samaria was deeply mixed, combining fear of the Lord with idol worship; this helps to explain later distrust against the Samaritans.
The nations in Samaria ended up practicing a hybrid religion, which the commentator calls the cult of "mestis" or mixed, ending the history of that earth.
The commentaries point out that the expression "today" points to the persistence of this pattern among the peoples set in Samaria, who feared the Lord without abandoning his own gods.

questions: What signs of infidelity to God appear in this chapter as more dangerous: the public sins or those practiced in secret?
Why does the text insist so much on the rejection of the prophets and the alliance, rather than explaining the fall only by political factors?
In what ways can a person or community today try to serve the Lord without abandoning competing idols?
study.practice: This chapter calls to spiritual integrity. Practical application is to examine whether our faith is mixed with rival loyalties: customs, practices, trust in other functional "gods," or selective obedience. It also invites us to take biblical warnings seriously before hardening becomes a habit. In concrete terms, it is worth abandoning what is incumbent with reverence for the LORD, to cultivate sincere repentance and to align worship, decisions and habits to the covenant of God.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify in detail some historical and textual points, such as the exact identity of certain localities and peoples mentioned in verses 24 to 31, nor do they fully explain the expression "costume of the God of that earth." They also do not allow to safely affirm the complete chronology of Hosea's reign beyond what the excerpts themselves mention. The reading of 17.41 as a main reference to the resettled peoples in Samaria is interpretive, although supported by the notes.
